front: Net present value (NPV) and its decision rule
back: NPV = sum of CF_t / (1+r)^t including the initial outlay at t = 0. Accept if NPV > 0. NPV is the expected change in firm value from the project.
The discount rate at which NPV = 0. Accept if IRR exceeds the required return (hurdle rate). Implicitly assumes reinvestment at the IRR; nonconventional cash flows can give multiple IRRs or none.
PI = PV of future cash flows / initial outlay = 1 + NPV/outlay. Accept if PI > 1. Measures NPV per unit of investment.
Ignores the time value of money and ignores all cash flows after the payback date. It is a rough gauge of liquidity and risk, not of profitability. Discounted payback fixes only the first problem.
CF = (S - C)(1 - T) + D x T, where D x T is the depreciation tax shield. Equivalent to net income + depreciation (excluding financing costs).

front: Which items are included or excluded in incremental cash flows?
back: Included: opportunity costs, externalities (cannibalization), change in net working capital, after-tax salvage. Excluded: sunk costs and financing costs (these are captured in the discount rate).

front: Why can NPV and IRR rank mutually exclusive projects differently?
back: Differences in project scale and in the timing of cash flows. Resolution: choose the project with the higher NPV.
The discount rate at which the NPVs of two projects are equal (where their NPV profiles intersect). It is the IRR of the difference in the two projects' cash flows.

front: Capital rationing: how should projects be chosen?
back: Choose the combination of projects that maximizes total NPV within the budget. Ranking by PI can be suboptimal when projects are indivisible.

front: Name the types of real options
back: Timing (delay), sizing (abandonment and expansion), flexibility (price-setting and production flexibility) and fundamental options. They add value that a static NPV misses.

front: Four stages of the capital allocation process
back: 1. Idea generation. 2. Analyzing proposals. 3. Capital allocation planning. 4. Monitoring and post-audit.

front: When does a positive-NPV project raise the share price?
back: Only to the extent that it is better than the market already expected. Value = PV of existing assets + NPV of future growth opportunities.
